attempts.error: The Antrieb managed cluster lease expired

evidence.finding: All four nodes reported wsrep_cluster_size=4, wsrep_local_state_comment=Synced, and identical appdb.orders COUNT(*)=5 — the 4-node Galera cluster with shared data was up and consistent across all members.

evidence.source: 15:14:46–15:18:56 apt-get purge/install commands on node2, node3, node4
evidence.finding: Three consecutive attempts to purge mariadb-server (10.0) and install mariadb-server-10.1 + rsync each timed out with 'AntriebMCPError: ... 120-second Proxy Read Timeout', run synchronously in the foreground rather than backgrounded per platform guidance.

Executor had to force-kill dpkg/debconf/apt-get processes left running after the timed-out installs, then repair the package state with dpkg --configure -a, before the cluster could be verified — direct evidence of disruption caused by the earlier synchronous install approach.

evidence.source: 15:25:07–15:25:49 reboot sequence on node4, then node3
evidence.finding: Both node4 and node3 were rebooted and successfully rejoined the cluster (Synced, Primary, cluster_size=4, correct data), confirming Galera auto-rejoin worked for at least 2 of 4 nodes.

Immediately after issuing the reboot command for node2 (the third node in the resilience test), the record shows outcome 'cluster_expired' with error 'The Antrieb managed cluster lease expired' — this is also the recorded termination cause for the whole attempt.

No SELECT/UPDATE/INSERT write command specifically targeting node4 appears in the selected evidence — only read-only COUNT(*) queries were run against it, so 'node4 accepts writes' is not directly demonstrated in the audit, only inferred from Galera's default multi-master behavior once a node reports wsrep_cluster_status=Primary.

likely_causes.cause: The attempt was terminated by cluster lease expiry (a session time/quota boundary), not by a functional defect in the cluster setup — the 4-node cluster was already Synced/Primary with consistent data at the last full observation.

Time was lost earlier in the session to three back-to-back apt-get purge/install commands that exceeded the 120s synchronous exec limit, followed by manual process-killing and dpkg repair across all four nodes. This ate into the session's time budget and likely contributed to the lease expiring during the reboot-resilience verification pass instead of after it.

Running the reboot-resilience check serially, node-by-node, at the very end of the session (node4, then node3, then node2 in progress) left no slack for the third/fourth node's verification before the lease ran out.

The default Ubuntu 16.04 mariadb-server package (10.0) was deemed insufficient and replaced with 10.1, suggesting either a version/package mis-selection early on or a deliberate upgrade — either way it required a disruptive purge+reinstall cycle across 3 nodes.

next_attempt_guidance: Decide the MariaDB/Galera package and version up front (check whether Ubuntu 16.04's default mariadb-server 10.0 supports wsrep/Galera adequately, or plan directly for a 10.1+ repo) to avoid a mid-run purge-and-reinstall across all data nodes.

Never run apt-get purge/install synchronously in the foreground when it may exceed ~120s; use the redirect+background+poll pattern (`cmd > /tmp/out.log 2>&1 & echo $! > pid; tail /tmp/out.log` in follow-up execs) as specified in the platform primer.

If an install does hang, confirm via `ps`/log tail that it's actually stuck (not just slow) before force-killing dpkg/debconf/apt processes; killing mid-transaction is what necessitated the dpkg --configure -a repair across 4 nodes.

After confirming cluster_size=4 / Synced / Primary with matching row counts, explicitly perform a write (INSERT/UPDATE) directed at node4 and re-verify it replicates to node1–3, to directly prove node4 'accepts writes like the other members' rather than relying on read-only checks.

Run reboot-resilience verification (if desired) earlier in the session or in parallel across nodes rather than serially at the end, so a lease/time boundary doesn't cut off verification partway through.

Track remaining session/lease time budget and prioritize confirming the core requirement (4-node cluster with shared data, node4 accepting writes) before spending remaining time on supplementary resilience testing like reboots.
diagnosis.summary: The redacted audit shows the core task was very likely achieved: by 15:25 UTC all four nodes (node1–4) independently reported wsrep_cluster_size=4, wsrep_local_state_comment=Synced, wsrep_cluster_status=Primary, and identical appdb.orders row counts, and node4 and node3 both successfully rejoined the cluster after a reboot. The attempt was not terminated by a technical failure in the cluster itself but by the Antrieb managed cluster lease expiring, which struck exactly as the executor issued a reboot to node2 as the third step of a serial reboot-resilience check. Earlier in the session, three synchronous apt-get purge/install commands (replacing mariadb-server 10.0 with 10.1) each hit the 120-second proxy timeout and required manual process-killing and dpkg repair across all nodes — this likely consumed session time that would otherwise have been available to complete verification before the lease expired. One evidence gap: no write operation specifically targeting node4 is present in the selected records, so 'node4 accepts writes' is inferred from Galera Primary state rather than directly observed.
